title: fleet/tools/lessons-check scans roster names and seat directories only under fleet/docs/lessons and never bead ids, so its rc 0 is not evidence for the epic's neutrality rule over fleet/ — and fleet/core/tests/dispatch.rs:27 already carries a seat directory it cannot see
description:
## Why

Every child of the fleet epic carries the rule that nothing under fleet/ names this repository, a roster seat's chosen name, a seat directory or a bead id, and names `python3 fleet/tools/lessons-check rc 0` as its proof. Read at 89faa2629 (tinytown-tnkuq.14's delivery), the tool's project-token scan (`tinytown`) runs over every tracked file under fleet/, but the roster-name and seat-directory scan runs only over fleet/docs/lessons/*.md (lessons-check:202-225), and no scan looks for a bead id at all. So a seat directory or a bead id in Rust source or a test passes the gate. Measured: `const BY: &str = "architect-1";` stands at fleet/core/tests/dispatch.rs:27 on the base and every delivery since, and the gate has been rc 0 throughout.

Found at the review of tinytown-tnkuq.14 (two readers named it independently); not that bead's to fix — the tool is the gate every fleet landing runs.

## Steps to Reproduce

From a worktree at 89faa2629 or later: `grep -n 'architect-1' fleet/core/tests/dispatch.rs` prints line 27; `python3 fleet/tools/lessons-check; echo rc=$?` prints rc=0. Plant `const X: &str = "builder-1";` in any fleet/**/*.rs and re-run: still rc 0. Expected after: rc 1 naming the file and line for both.

## What lands

lessons-check widens the roster-name and seat-directory scan to every tracked file under fleet/ (the same set the project-token scan walks) and adds a bead-id scan (the `tinytown-` prefix already covers ids; a project-neutral form is `<prefix>-[a-z0-9.]+` read from the tool's own configuration), with the allowlist the lessons documents need for their `Test:` lines. The existing hit at fleet/core/tests/dispatch.rs:27 is rewritten to a generic actor in the same landing so the gate is green on landing.

## Acceptance Criteria

Written at the spec pass. Minimum: a planted `builder-1` in a .rs file under fleet/ reds the tool; a planted bead id reds it; the tree at landing is rc 0; the tool's own suite (if any) green; make fleet-test rc 0.

title: A usage limit reached mid-flight: measure what the agent leaves in its transcript, then the adapter's limit-reached state, the flight holding every remaining dispatch with one dispatch.failed, and the resume on a probe (flights PRD R13 widened; Flights Under Stress scenario 2)
description:
## Why

Found by the stress test of the flights PRD (the "Flights Under Stress" page, scenario 2, 2026-09-09): the PRD covers a logged-out FIRST turn (R13: dispatch.failed, the item held, three in a row halt dispatching) and a usage reading pinned at takeoff (Q1), but a seat that reaches the account's usage limit MID-turn has no signal. It stalls or exits; the flight reads that as a crash (the crashed-seat decide bead) or as silence, and every fresh dispatch after it fails the same way at the prompt floor's cost. Gas City restarts such a session every tick at ~36K tokens a start until an undocumented hold (gas-city.md G13, G14, G21).

## What

- Measure first, on the pinned agent version: what a session that hits the usage limit mid-turn leaves in its transcript and its exit — a named line, a usage field, an exit code — through the adapter's transcript verb. The measurement is the first deliverable and is written on this bead before any code.
- Then: the adapter reports limit-reached as a session state the controller can read; the flight's advance, on seeing it for any seat, holds every remaining dispatch with one dispatch.failed naming the limit (not one per item), retires nothing it does not have to, and resumes dispatching on the tick when a probe answers; the flight's summary carries the held span.
- The PRD's R13 widened to name the mid-turn case, marked constant for the signal and key for the probe interval.

## Acceptance

- The measurement quoted on the bead, with the version.
- A fixture: a transcript carrying the measured limit shape reads as limit-reached through the adapter; the advance under it dispatches nothing across ten ticks and writes exactly one dispatch.failed; a probe answering clears the hold.
- Gate: touched suites green (fleetmake rows); reviewer runs the full suite at landing.

The flight half (holding every remaining dispatch, dispatch.failed, resume on a probe) is the core run lifecycle's after the workflows sitting, not fly's; build the adapter half first and re-read the second against the run lifecycle's spec.

title: Design session: fleet-log and fleet-stats, one PRD — the record as a product (retention, export, the SSE reader) and the numbers folded over it (the default set, its derivations, track-your-own, cost); settled: the stream is the only store and stats is a fold over it (Alberto's call 2026-09-08)
description:
## Why

The vision page names two pieces with no PRD: fleet-log, "the single event stream every other piece writes to … one format, one place, so third-party tools plug into fleet once and every piece shows up," and fleet-stats, "the numbers that matter for a factory: how far each seat can go before it needs to rest, what a landing costs, how often work comes back, how long a flight takes, and how each agent compares on all of it. A default set ships with fleet. Track your own beside them. If the manager is installed, stats is a tab in it." The controller PRD defines the stream's file, envelope and vocabulary (R25) and calls it fleet-log's first writer; nothing designs the log as a product — retention, export, what a person searches a month later, the incidents collector and the row-moves journal it lists at P1 — and nothing designs the numbers. Alberto's call in architect-2's session, 2026-09-08: one PRD for both, because they are one story — stats has no input but the log.

## Settled before the sitting, from the record

- The stream is the record and the only one: every stat is a fold over events, never a second store (controller PRD principle five; the cli PRD's exit and read-back rules).
- The stream carries what a person asks about — a crash, a nudge, an adoption, a hold, a landing, a return, a cost — and never the controller's own housekeeping (lessons G17, measured: 540 of 676 rows on an idle reference instance were housekeeping).
- The transport for a live reader is SSE with fifteen-second heartbeats and ids equal to the sequence (lessons G18; controller PRD P1); fleet event tail --since is the same cursor at the shell.
- The reference's scoreboard is the shape stats distills (R): keys with a stated derivation, per-landing deltas rather than standing totals, a drift alarm at three MAD over a week, re-baselined by append with the space each line was computed in stamped on it.
- The manager's API, if published, is generated from the cli's Rust types, a handful of paths, loopback by default, over the projection and the stream (Alberto's ruling 2026-09-08, on the manager's design bead).

## What the sitting decides

The log-and-stats PRD, in fleet/docs/prds beside the other four, from a design session with Alberto and an architect. Lettered on this bead at the sitting's start:

- Q1 Retention and rotation of events.jsonl: never, by size, by age; what a rotated file is named and whether tail reads across the seam.
- Q2 Export for third parties: the JSONL file, the SSE endpoint, both; whether an export envelope strips anything (the reference's public envelope hashed the actor and stripped the payload, lessons G17, which made it useless to a manager).
- Q3 The default stat set and each key's derivation, written once: context before rest, landing cost, return rate, flight duration, per-agent comparison — which events each folds over and in what window.
- Q4 Where stats are computed and read: on the controller's tick into the projection, by a verb the cli PRD does not list (a stats verb would be a new ruling), or by the manager alone; and whether a stat is ever written back to the stream.
- Q5 "Track your own": how a pack or a project declares a stat — a file in a slot, a key in fleet.toml — and how a declared stat reaches the manager's tab.
- Q6 The incidents collector and the row-moves journal (controller PRD P1): whether they are stats, log readers, or neither.
- Q7 Cost: which event carries token cost and who writes it, since the reference stream carried none (G17) and "what a flight cost" is on the vision page.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1 fleet/docs/prds/fleet-log-and-stats-prd.md landed in the shape of the PRDs beside it, carrying the settled list above under Recorded directions, the seven questions ruled with their letters, and no reference to this repository.
- AC2 every name the PRD introduces has a row in fleet/docs/naming.md (log and stats are already there).
- AC3 the frames the PRD's first slice needs filed under the fleet epic and placed as the sitting rules.
- Gate: touched suites green (lessons-check, doctrine-drift); reviewer runs the full suite, ran or cached, at landing.

covers: none — a design session; the requirements are the PRD's to number
notes:
LANDSCAPE SURVEY (architect-2, 2026-09-08T19:48Z, for the sitting; the Claude Code facts read from code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage the same day, the rest from the reference's own measurements in fleet/docs/lessons/gas-city.md and general knowledge of the tools named):
- Every lasting system has five things: an append-only log whose sequence is the cursor (journald's cursor, Kafka's offset, Redis Streams' entry id, Bazel BEP's per-build sequence, Gas City's seq as the SSE id); retention by size or age with rotation the cursor survives (journald, Kafka); numbers as declared folds over the log in one place and never a second store (Prometheus recording rules, Kafka stream processors, Bazel build scans); a typed envelope with a subject so a fold can filter; and one standard export as the plug-in point, today OpenTelemetry (one collector, any backend).
- Q1 lead: copy the journal — rotate by size, name the rotated file by its first and last sequence, let fleet event tail read across the seam.
- Q2 lead: export the stream as OpenTelemetry log records over OTLP, off by default; the reference's public envelope that hashed the actor and stripped the payload (G17) is the mistake to avoid.
- Q3/Q4 lead: stats are folds declared once (the reference scoreboard's shape: stated derivation, per-landing deltas, the 3-MAD drift alarm, re-baseline by append), computed on demand or on the tick; no stats verb before the definitions exist; the manager's tab is the reader.
- Q7 answer from the provider: Claude Code, with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, exports claude_code.cost.usage (USD) and claude_code.token.usage (tokens) with attributes model, query_source, agent.name, skill.name, plugin.name, and an event claude_code.api_request carrying cost_usd, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens and cache_creation_tokens per request, over OTLP grpc/http, Prometheus or console; session.id on every metric. So cost is collected from the provider by the adapter (the controller starts each session with telemetry pointed at a collector), never estimated by fleet; a second provider's adapter answers it its own way — the overlay seam.
- Left out on purpose: a query language (grep and DuckDB over JSONL exist), a stripping export envelope, any stats verb ahead of the folds.
Q5 LEAD (architect-2, 2026-09-08T19:53Z, answering Alberto's "how would a user add a stat to track?" in session): two forms and no expression language. (1) Declare a fold as a [stats.<name>] table in fleet.toml — the file that already carries [guards] and [gates] — with a fixed grammar: description, unit, one event type or a numerator/denominator pair for a rate, an optional payload field to fold (else a count), a fold from a short list (count, sum, median, last, rate), a window from a short list (per landing, per flight, rolling Nd), an optional actor filter, an optional drift-alarm opt-in; anything outside the form is refused at load naming the key, as an order file is. Core ships the default set as the same table in its own policy file; a pack adds or overrides by name through last-wins merge; a person's fleet.toml sits above both. (2) Emit an event when the number is not derivable: any command can append stat.observed {name, value, unit} — an order's exec on a schedule, a skill at a ritual's end, a person's script — and the declared fold over it is last or sum filtered by name, so a custom stat is a log line like everything else and survives rotation. Every declared stat lands in the projection's stats array with value, window and the sequence computed through; fleet status prints it and the manager's tab reads it. Refused: an expression language, a stat from anything but the stream, a stats verb ahead of the definitions.
PRIOR WORK: jklenk/thread (architect-2, 2026-09-08T19:57Z, read from github.com/jklenk/thread at Alberto's ask — README, thread/schema.sql, thread/actor_classifier.py). A read-only forensics and analytics layer for Beads in Python: extracts bd's Dolt commit history into a DuckDB file (.beads/thread.duckdb) as one row per field change, derives per-item lifecycle facts, and prints a plain-language health summary (thread prime), a self-contained HTML report (Chart.js) and ad-hoc SQL (thread query). Non-goals match ours: not a UI, not a daemon, not a planner. Worth borrowing, for the sitting:
- The insight: bd's Dolt history IS an event log of the work graph — every status, assignee, dependency and note change, with actor and time — and fleet's stream carries none of it. Sharpens Q4: item stats (return rate, reopen, cycle time, queue wait, late-added blockers) can be folded from the graph's own history read-only, so the stream need not carry item.* events for stats; the verbs write their notes and the graph is the record of the item, as the principle already says for bd. The sitting rules which store each default stat folds over.
- Metrics with plain names and stated formulas: fidelity = 1 − min(1, reopens·0.4 + revisions·0.4 + rejected·0.2) — our returns-per-delivery in another vocabulary; rework cost = reopens·2 + revisions·1.5 + rejected·1 + compaction·1 + agent_actors·0.5, wall-clock excluded on purpose because agent work sits idle between claim and close (a rule fleet should keep); queue wait (time to start); late-add items (created and claimed within 5 s mid-session) and late-add blockers (a dependency added after first claim = a replan); dependency-order violations (a blocked item closed before its blocker); spec-quality correlation (has acceptance criteria vs cycle time and wait — the harness's own bet, measured); priority and type performance. Each is a fold over graph history in the [stats] grammar or a named default.
- Principles: orphans participate in scoring (LEFT JOIN everywhere); plain outcome language, no data-model words in what a person reads; the item is the atomic unit and agents are disposable — observe patterns, never infer intent; thresholds labelled "v1 hypotheses, not ground truth" with the sample they came from (34 issues, April 2026) — the honesty our scoreboard's re-baseline-by-append rule already has.
- Ad hoc questions answered by DuckDB over the files with a documented recipe rather than a query language of fleet's own — the Q3 answer for anything outside the default set, no crate in core.
Not borrowed: the actor classifier (fleet's actor is the seat name; their behavioural cascade exists because bd does not know who is an agent); DuckDB as a dependency of fleet-core; 25 SQL views as a product surface; Gas Town-specific signals (compaction, hop_uri, role_type).
DIRECTION (architect-2, 2026-09-17, tinytown-tnkuq.92): the event log is a feature-layer piece on fleet/docs/fleet-layers.md, and the stream gains a load the sitting did not price: a code workflow's durability (fleet-layers Q8, recommended: replay from the stream). The retention and export questions here are re-read with that consumer in mind at the workflows sitting; this PRD follows it.
Moved from the tinytown board on 2026-09-22, where it was tinytown-tnkuq.38; that bead is closed there with a pointer here. Edges to beads that stayed on the tinytown board, not carried across: relates-to tinytown-tnkuq.32.
POST-SPLIT CORRECTION (2026-09-23 sweep, checked against HEAD 44c3736). Reparented under fleet-wnt. No log/stats PRD and no stats code exist. The only related ruling is 'stats' as an API read path (brain/fleet-layers.md:216). Retention and rotation are now constrained by replay from the stream (the replay contract :327, Q8 :631). Same path and gate fixes as .37.

title: Design session: the fleet manager — the one piece with a network surface; settled before the sitting: an API, if published, is generated from the cli's own Rust types (utoipa or equivalent), a handful of paths, loopback by default, over the projection and the event stream (Alberto's ruling 2026-09-08)
description:
## Why

The vision page names fleet-manager as the part nothing else has: a single view of the fleet — what is in the air, what landed, what is blocked, what needs you — with decisions arriving as questions with options, answerable from a desk or a phone, and the door to the premium tier. The controller PRD declines any HTTP surface in the daemon (its non-goals: no UI, no HTTP surface, no dashboard; the manager reads the projection and the events the daemon writes), and the cli PRD's surface serves nothing over a network. So the manager is the one piece that needs a network surface, and its design has no PRD. The engine trial of 2026-09-05 measured the reference's surface (lessons G18: an SSE endpoint on loopback with fifteen-second heartbeats and resumable ids, an OpenAPI 3.1.0 document of 127 paths and 700 KB, a same-origin dashboard; G6: an API broader than its CLI) and fleet copied the transport into the controller PRD's P1 and declined the rest.

## Settled before the sitting

Alberto's ruling, 2026-09-08, in architect-2's session, verbatim: "If fleet publishes one, it should be generated from the same Rust types the cli uses, with a crate such as utoipa deriving the schema from the handlers, so the cli and the API cannot disagree, and it should be a handful of paths, loopback by default, over the two files that are already the record."

The seat's reading: one definition of the surface, in Rust types, from which the cli's verbs and the API's paths are both derived, so neither can drift from the other; the schema document generated from the handlers (utoipa or its equivalent) and never hand-written; the path count small enough to read in one sitting; loopback unless a person turns exposure on; and every read served from the projection and the event stream, the two files the controller already writes — no third store, no belief the stream cannot reproduce. The SSE transport of the controller PRD's P1 (heartbeats every fifteen seconds, ids equal to the stream's sequence, the same envelope as the stored event) is the stream's network form, and fleet event tail's --since is its resumable id.

## What the sitting decides

The manager PRD, in fleet/docs/prds beside the other three, from a design session with Alberto and an architect. The questions it settles, each lettered on this bead at the sitting's start so the report card can carry them:

- Q1 Where the manager runs: a verb of the one binary (a serve verb, which the cli PRD does not list and would add), a fourth crate producing a second binary, or a separate product that only reads the two files.
- Q2 The read paths: which handful — the projection, the stream over SSE, one item's record, the decisions owed — and which of them the cli already answers so that the definition is shared.
- Q3 Writes, if any: whether the API carries any verb (dispatch, fly, autopilot on|off, an answer to a decision) or is read-only with the phone answering decisions through the work graph.
- Q4 Exposure: loopback by default; what turns the network on, and what authenticates it when it is on.
- Q5 The screen: what the first view shows, and whether it ships as a page the daemon serves, a page in the artifact tool, or a native shell.
- Q6 The premium line: which of the above is the door the vision page names.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1 fleet/docs/prds/fleet-manager-prd.md landed in the shape of the three PRDs beside it, carrying the settled paragraph above verbatim under Recorded directions, the six questions ruled with their letters, and no reference to this repository.
- AC2 every name the PRD introduces has a row in fleet/docs/naming.md.
- AC3 the frames the PRD's first slice needs filed under the fleet epic and placed on the departure board or beyond it, as the sitting rules.
- Gate: touched suites green (lessons-check, doctrine-drift); reviewer runs the full suite, ran or cached, at landing.

covers: none — a design session; the requirements are the PRD's to number
notes:
RULING RECORDED (architect-2, 2026-09-08T18:58Z): the settled paragraph in the description is Alberto's ruling of 2026-09-08 verbatim, indexed on the epic under mechanism manager-api-shape. This bead is a sitting with Alberto; it is not dispatched to a builder and sits off the departure board, which is phase A's; the manager is the piece after it.
SITTING OPENED (Alberto, 2026-09-09, in architect-2's session, verbatim): "here's what i have defined for the manager/cockpit at this point. im currently leaning towards naming it cockpit, thoughts? a web app wrapped with tauri and also a server that exposes a typed API, correct so far? the app by itself should have an empty state, some status items alongside the bottom (account usage limits, controller status, etc) and a settings screen. that's it. i will provide mocks for all of this before implementation since i want it to be highly polished and thought-through so no need to dwell on the ui at this point. the settings screen is a UI window into the fleet.toml, any changes on that screen probably edits the toml file without committing anything. an additional piece of settings here that will come way down the road is a way to switch between provider accounts automatically when usage runs out. this is something i have to do manually now but it would be great to have it handled. this also touches on the economy factor. if we know how much runway you have based on your account(s) information we can warn you against changing it to LG or we also limit how many concurrent flights you can fly if you're trying to make it to the end of the week without running out of gas. so that's it, that's the cockpit at its most basic, the cockpit equivalent of the core pack: an empty state screen, a customizable bar with status, gauges, alerts, etc, and a settings screen with project and account config, and then eventually maybe fleet account stuff if we have a cloud offering. im leaving out the main piece of this which we can discuss next after you process this." The seat's reading against the lettered questions: Q5 (the screen) is answered in shape — a web app in a Tauri shell, first view an empty state, a status bar, a settings screen, mocks to come from Alberto before any build; Q1 (where it runs) is half answered — a Tauri app and a server with a typed API, with where the server process lives still open; Q4 keeps loopback by default. New matter the questions did not carry: settings as a live window on fleet.toml (edits written, never committed); provider-account switching on exhaustion, way down the road; an economy reading from account usage that warns and caps concurrent flights against a horizon. The main piece is withheld until the next turn.
SURVEY OPENED (architect-2, 2026-09-09, at Alberto's word in the sitting): before the UI walk, a landscape read of how tools let end users and their agents define custom views while holding an app-level style — where each draws the line between freedom and consistency and by what mechanism. Alberto's framing verbatim: "i want every end user and their agent to build whatever ui they want on top of fleet. we give them the primitives and the theme and components they can use to build the ui. i want whatever they build to still adhere to a style set at the app level. i dont want it to just be an iframe with totally different styles between views. this is where our research should focus, how do other tools draw the line between freedom and consistency." Corpus, fetched from official docs by four sonnet-class subagents in parallel under the builder-subagent-economy authorization, the seat verifying load-bearing claims itself before ruling on them: VS Code and Zed; pi.dev, Obsidian and Raycast; Grafana, Home Assistant and Backstage; Atlassian Forge, Shopify, Slack Block Kit and Figma plugins. The synthesis is the seat's and goes on this bead when written.
SURVEY FINDINGS (architect-2, 2026-09-09; twelve tools, four subagent passes, four load-bearing quotes re-fetched by the seat: Raycast "You concentrate on the logic, we push the pixels. Use our built-in UI components to be consistent with all our extensions"; Atlassian UI Kit "You also still cannot use arbitrary HTML, and are restricted to using the components exported from @forge/react"; Shopify Built for Shopify 4.1.1 rejection reasons "Button styles do not match the Shopify admin", "The majority of content does not reside in card-like containers", "Body text size is significantly different", "An app's background color is significantly different"; pi.dev extensions apply the theme by explicit theme.fg() calls in render callbacks — the pass's sentence "custom UI does not automatically use theme colors" was NOT on the page and is not relied on).
THE SPECTRUM, five rungs by mechanism:
1 schema only, host renders every pixel — Slack Block Kit (JSON; one style enum on buttons, primary|danger; 50 blocks a message, 100 a modal), VS Code tree views (TreeDataProvider, "conforms to the style of the built-in views"), Home Assistant built-in cards (YAML), Zed (no custom UI surface at all; the request sits open labelled as an infrastructure gap).
2 component kit as the only surface, no DOM and no CSS — Raycast (React, but List, Grid, Detail, Form and ActionPanel only; a typed Color API; the store rejects a view that swaps content where a push was expected and a custom settings screen), Atlassian Forge UI Kit (@forge/react components in a managed runtime; tokens on automatically).
3 in-process code composing the host's kit with a theme object, policed by rule or review — Grafana ("Always use components from @grafana/ui", "Never hardcode visual properties like colors, spacing, padding, or font sizes", custom CSS only through Emotion over useStyles2), Backstage ("strongly urge", explicitly not mandatory; two theme systems mid-migration, MUI object and --bui-* variables, "not ideal" in their own words), pi.dev (its own TUI primitives — Text, Box, Container, Markdown, SelectList, ScrollView and the rest — with the theme passed as a parameter the extension applies).
4 free DOM or web component in the page, theme as CSS variables, opt-in — Obsidian (hundreds of variables in five families; the guideline says hardcoded styling "makes it impossible to modify with themes and snippets"; review, not runtime), Home Assistant custom cards (any framework except React; the official page names no shared element library and no variable to use; the community built card-mod to reach into cards' shadow DOM), Shopify (an iframe, but Polaris ships as web components so using the kit is the theming; nothing gates the App Store, and the Built for Shopify tier scores looks).
5 free iframe, theme as CSS variables, opt-in — VS Code webviews (--vscode-* variables and body classes; "used sparingly and only when VS Code's native API is inadequate"; the Webview UI Toolkit archived 2025-01-06 when its FAST dependency was abandoned), Figma plugins (themeColors: true injects 200+ variables; "we highly recommend matching your plugin or widget to Figma's UI"; review rules never mention looks), Atlassian Custom UI (view.theme.enable(), recommended).
THE FINDINGS:
F1 No host on rungs 4 and 5 enforces consistency by any mechanism but words — recommend, strongly urge, sparingly — and the famous failures live there: off-theme webviews, Home Assistant needing card-mod, Backstage's two theme systems. Consistency is enforced only where there is no escape hatch (rungs 1 and 2) or where a review gate scores looks (Shopify's top tier, Raycast's store).
F2 Every host that offers freedom offers it BESIDE a constrained tier, as a named choice, and steers to the constrained one by default: Atlassian UI Kit vs Custom UI, VS Code tree view vs webview, Home Assistant built-in card vs custom card.
F3 Three ways the theme reaches a view: CSS variables (Obsidian, Figma, VS Code, Backstage new, Home Assistant), a JS theme object (Grafana, pi.dev, Backstage legacy), typed component props (Raycast). Variables are the web's own mechanism and outlive any framework; all three are opt-in by nature unless the kit is the only surface.
F4 Where the kit is the enforcement, the kit's completeness is the freedom budget: Raycast's four root views, Block Kit's ceilings, and Atlassian's "known limitations" page exist because a kit is never everything; the constrained tier stays honest only if it grows with demand.
F5 Kits die with their substrate: VS Code's toolkit died of a dependency. Web components (Shopify Polaris, Home Assistant) are the framework-agnostic shape; a kit bound to one framework is a bet on that framework.
F6 For an agent, the shapes rank: a declarative document (Block Kit's "sculpting specially-structured JSON") is what an agent writes best and what a check can verify with an exit code; code composing a kit is second and needs a build; free HTML is the easiest to write and the only one nothing checks.
F7 fleet has no store and no review gate, so a line held by review (Shopify, Raycast, Obsidian, Grafana) is not available; the line must be structural (no escape hatch) or instrumented (a check that refuses a view carrying a raw color, font or size — the guard pattern applied to views).
THE SEAT'S RECOMMENDATION for fleet, offered for ruling and not ruled: two tiers and no iframe. Tier one, views as declarative documents over a cockpit block vocabulary (list, table, board, gauge, timeline, detail, form, markdown, action) bound to the API's typed paths and stream queries, rendered by the cockpit, validated by a check verb, shippable in a pack — Block Kit's shape with Raycast's rigor, and the shape an agent writes and verifies best. Tier two, custom components as web components composed from the cockpit's own component library and tokens, in the page and never in a frame, with a check that refuses raw visual values — Grafana's "never hardcode" made an instrument instead of a sentence. Declined by recommendation: an iframe tier (F1: every host that has one has the failure Alberto named).
DATE CORRECTION (architect-2, 2026-09-08T22:33Z read from date -u): every note this seat wrote on this record today carrying the date 2026-09-09 — the rulings vision-primitives-not-features, cockpit-is-the-name, cockpit-server-in-the-binary, cockpit-serve-and-launch, cockpit-economy-warning, cockpit-read-paths, cockpit-writes, cockpit-exposure, cockpit-premium-line and cockpit-view-line on the epic, the sitting-opened, survey-opened and survey-findings notes on fleet-tnkuq.37, and the description and verdict on tinytown-tnkuq.39 — was written on 2026-09-08 between roughly 20:30Z and 22:30Z. The date was taken from the harness's own "today" line instead of the clock; the clock reads 2026-09-08. The content of every note stands; only the date in each is wrong by one day.
SITTING ADDENDUM (Alberto, 2026-09-08T22:39Z, in architect-2's session, verbatim): "something i forgot to mention earlier is a fourth piece of the cockpit is the roster. so roster, empty page, status, and settings. the roster lists all the named seats and allows user to open a tmux window with the conversation." The seat's reading: the cockpit at its most basic is four pieces — the roster, the empty page, the status bar, the settings screen. The roster is a view over the projection's seat rows (fleet status --json per seat: state, last verdict, context against the threshold, the item held), listing the named seats with spawned seats shown as transient rather than hidden. Opening the conversation is a human sitting in a live session, which the controller PRD holds at P2 as "a per-seat attach for a human to sit in a session from the manager" — this pulls it into the cockpit's first slice. It decomposes onto the seams: an eighth adapter verb, attach, provider-specific (Claude Code's own attach for its sessions; the trial's Gas City ran seats in tmux panes), so the controller PRD's seven verbs become eight; a cli verb fleet seat attach <seat> under the done-to noun, which the cockpit calls and a person can run bare; the terminal it opens in is a policy key with tmux as the first implementation and never a hard dependency; and one event, session.attached with the actor as the person, so the morning's record shows a human spoke in a seat's session. Rulings owed at the PRD: whether the roster is a tab or the empty page's own content, and whether the attach opens the user's tmux server, a new terminal window, or a pane inside the cockpit — the last one is the P2 attach the vision page implies and is the largest shape.

title: fleet dispatch's one-item-at-a-time check counts every open item assigned to the seat, so a stale assignee (an epic, an untouched old bug) blocks dispatch; count only ordered items, the way held_item does
description:
## What

core/src/item/dispatch.rs:202-214 refuses a named seat that holds ANY open or in_progress item assigned to it. core/src/item/deliver.rs:272-289 held_item, which answers the same question ('which item is this seat carrying'), counts only items whose record has an orders key. The two readers disagree. At the switch sitting (tinytown-tnkuq.23, 2026-09-22T16:54Z), 'fleet dispatch … --to builder-1' was refused with 'builder-1 already holds tinytown-6ravv (open), tinytown-hxn (open)'. The first was an epic still carrying a previous operator as assignee, the second a P3 bug assigned a month earlier and untouched. Neither had been dispatched. Alberto ruled 2026-09-23 (post-split review triage): count ordered items only.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1 Dispatch's hold check counts only open or in_progress items that carry an orders key, and never an epic. It shares its reading with held_item rather than keeping a second one.
- AC2 An arm where the seat is assigned an unordered open item and an epic, and dispatch proceeds. An arm where the seat holds an ordered item, and dispatch still refuses by name. The first arm is shown red against today's code.
- AC3 The refusal text still names each held item and its status.

title: fleet deliver accepts a note with a second column-zero marker below line 1, then commits, reassigns and writes the note before its own read-back fails
description:
## What

`grammar_holds` (core/src/item/deliver.rs:404-427) checks only that the first line opens on a marker, plus the labels. The walk then commits (:143-150), assigns, writes `store.note` (:172), and only then runs `read_back` (:179). `last_region` anchors on the LAST column-zero marker (`rposition`, core/src/item/mod.rs:550). So a re-delivery that quotes the superseded `DELIVERED <sha>` at column zero, or any column-zero ACCEPTED, LANDED, PARKED or ANSWERED line in the body, fails the read-back after the commit, the reviewer assignment and the note have all happened, with no event and no ring. `last_region` does not track code fences either, so packs/tiny/assets/manual.md:53-54 ('indented or fenced') is wrong about fences. Verdicts already refuse this (`off_column_zero`, core/src/item/review.rs:536); deliveries do not.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1 Deliver refuses, before committing, a note with any region marker at column zero below its first line. The refusal names the line and the fix (indent it).
- AC2 A plain delivery, and a re-delivery that quotes nothing, still pass.
- AC3 The manual's 'or fenced' is corrected, or the reader learns fences.
- AC4 A core/tests/deliver.rs arm that goes red when the check is removed.

## Source

Carried from tinytown-7k5ef (the bd-notes-guard first-line-marker hole) (closed on the tinytown board at the 2026-09-22 post-harness sweep; listed in tinyfleet-review.md), triaged against tinyfleet HEAD 44c3736 on 2026-09-23.

description:
## What

Tinytown's exact trigger (no --project and an unreadable configured project) no longer fires, because cli/src/main.rs:1165-1183 returns None there. It still fires whenever `--project <listed>` is typed or the configured project is listed.

- AC1 A help flag given to the command itself allows, per tool, and only where that tool means help: `-h` is a value flag for gsutil (STORAGE_VALUE_FLAGS, :98).

* AC2 twenty quiet runs of the binary read 0 LEAK after the fix, or the bead closes as measured-and-explained with the rate left as found.

title: drive rig: the patient rigs' worst case under the attempt floor exceeds the runner's own timeout — three discarded 60 s attempts is 180 s against the profile's 80 s x 2, so that storm is killed by nextest without the rig's refusal ever being written
description:
## Why

Luggage off tinytown-5l61b's landing (67b020fbe). The rig's patience became a floor of STUB_START_ATTEMPTS = 3 tries OR a ceiling of 10 s of attempt time, and the three patient rigs in fleet/cli/tests/drive_children.rs run on PATIENT_DEADLINE_MS = 60_000. A storm that discards three patient attempts in a row costs up to 3 x 60 s = 180 s, while fleet/.config/nextest.toml bounds an arm at an 80 s period x 2 = 160 s: the runner's TIMEOUT lands before the rig's refusal, so the one red that should carry the attempts-and-calm figures is a bare kill. title: A live session the controller's table does not name is never adopted, so a porter-started session pays one revive (one wake) at its first hibernation before the hold can take it — adoption claims only rows a dispatch or a revive wrote; retires at the switch, or earlier by claiming any live row on a seat's own worktree
description:
## Why

tinytown-06kcv's post-landing live read (its POST-LANDING LIVE READ note, 2026-09-21): a foreground controller polled twelve times beside the porter's four live idle seats and adopted none, because fleet/controller/src/effect.rs's adopt iterates the session table's rows and claims the live row of a session the table already names; ~/.fleet/sessions.json named none of today's four porter-started session ids. So the hold tinytown-06kcv built cannot take a session until this controller has dispatched or revived it once: a porter-started session hibernates (about sixty minutes idle on Claude Code 2.1.261), decide's 5c revives it (one wake), the revive writes its row, and from the next live sighting on it is adopted and held. One wake per porter-started session, once — bounded, and gone at the switch (tinytown-tnkuq.23), after which every session is the fleet's own dispatch and is in the table from birth.

## What lands (if flown before the switch)

1. A decision first, on this bead: whether adoption may claim a live row the table does not name when the row's cwd is a seat's own worktree (gas-city G7 reads "every live session it names" — the widening is fleet's, and the 2026-09-21 landing narrowed the old pid-less widening back; a live-row widening is a different claim and needs its own measurement of what else could stand on a seat's worktree with a pid).
2. If ruled yes: the sighting writes a table row for a live listed session on a seat's worktree, and adopt claims it on the same poll; one arm on the adoption rig (a live idle row on the owned worktree with NO table row is claimed, session.adopted once) and the mutant that skips the write reds it.

## Acceptance Criteria

• AC1 the decision recorded in the keyed grammar before any build.
• AC2 the arm green; the mutant red, read from the arm's own failure line.
• AC3 cd fleet && cargo nextest run -p fleet-controller -E 'binary(adoption) + binary(effects)' rc 0 bare and under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.claude.
• Gate: touched suites green; reviewer runs the full suite, ran or cached, at landing.

## Risk

Adoption's claim widens to sessions this controller never started; the worktree match is what keeps it to the fleet's seats. Nothing lands if the switch comes first.

RULING (Alberto, 2026-09-21, AskUserQuestion in architect-1's session at 2026-09-21T23:14:07Z read from date -u, mechanism: porter-started-session-pays-one-revive-until-the-switch, verbatim): "B — leave it bounded (Recommended)"

title: Two fleet-cli::ring_flight arms hung silently to the 660 s cap on a quiet box at tinytown-tnkuq.104's landing gates (the_foreground_loop_leaves_the_same_stream_as_the_tick, then a_loop_killed_between_a_dispatch_and_its_event_restarts_without_dispatching_twice on the rerun) — the ring's stalls carry no reading before the cap kills them; bound the waits and print the flight's state on expiry
description:
## What was seen

At the re-prepared landing gate of tinytown-tnkuq.104 on flight tinytown-6bphr (land branch 244b01a69 over origin/main 41dcc2ce5, gate started 2026-09-18T10:22Z, box quiet at load 4.2, nothing else running), fleet-ring read 15 arms, 14 passed, 1 timed out:

    TIMEOUT [660.003s] (7/15) fleet-cli::ring_flight the_foreground_loop_leaves_the_same_stream_as_the_tick
    Summary [1397.103s] 15 tests run: 14 passed, 1 timed out

The ring profile runs its arms serially (test-threads = 1), so no neighbour loaded it. The ring profile's junit (target/nextest/ring/junit.xml, copied before the rerun overwrote it) holds the arm's whole output: the single libtest line "has been running for over 60 seconds" and nothing else — no assertion, no panic, no stderr. The same diff read fleet-ring 15 green at 09:17Z the same day, as did every other ring run on this flight. The .104 diff touches core's run verb and the cli's run subcommand and nothing on the flight or fly path.

The arm (fleet/cli/tests/ring_flight.rs:1653) has two halves: a ticked flight driven by tick_until_closed with a bound of 60, and a foreground flight driven by the shipped binary's own fly loop, which by the arm's own comment "runs the same pass until the flight closes" — with no deadline in the arm and, as far as the arm shows, none in the binary. A flight that never closes in that half is an arm that hangs until nextest's 660 s cap kills it, and the arm's silence says which half only by elimination: the ticked half is bounded.

## What this bead asks

Find what stalled: reproduce with the rig's stderr captured per pass (the fly loop's own refusal lines, the stub agent's calls), and bound the foreground half — a deadline on the arm's fly call with the flight's status and the builder log quoted on expiry, so a stall is a red with a reading instead of a silent timeout. If the stall is the binary's (a fly loop that can park or wait forever with no collector), that is its own finding on the fly verb.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1 the cause of the 660 s stall is named on this bead from a captured reproduction, or the arm is bounded and its next stall prints the flight's status and the builder log before failing.
- AC2 the arm is green ten of ten under make fleet-ring on a quiet box, each run's wall time recorded.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a quiet box (uptime 1-minute load under 5.0, nothing else of the fleet running), from a worktree at origin/main 244b01a69 or later, run: eval "$(tools/toolchain-env --export)"; make fleet-ring.
2. Read the ring's Summary line and any TIMEOUT rows; on 2026-09-18 two of three runs timed one arm out at 660 s (the_foreground_loop_leaves_the_same_stream_as_the_tick at 10:22Z, a_loop_killed_between_a_dispatch_and_its_event_restarts_without_dispatching_twice at 11:01Z) and the third read 15 green.
3. Read fleet/target/nextest/ring/junit.xml for the timed-out arm: its system-out holds one libtest line and nothing else, which is the finding.

On flight tinytown-6bphr — luggage, filed by the operator (architect-1) at the tinytown-tnkuq.104 re-prepared gate, 2026-09-18T11:02:23Z. STOWED, UNFED at this window; rides to the desk on the flight report as stowed-unfed. Not ordered: no orders key, no feed marker.

Its junit output is the same single libtest line and nothing else. The whole ring took 1518.8 s. The a_loop_killed arm is the one flight tinytown-6bphr's manifest already records at 660 s under a loaded gate and 72 s alone the night before; today it hit the cap alone. Every fleet/ source the ring binaries compile is byte-identical between this land branch and the tree that read fleet-ring 15 green at 09:17Z the same day (git diff empty over fleet/ less docs but for fleet/cli/tests/seat.rs, which is not a ring binary) — so the ring's two silent timeouts today are the box's or the arms' own timing, not a tree change. title: The controller's run pass does not latch a seam refusal: a re-run that cannot run is asked for again every poll with the refusal repeating on stderr, where the park and the cleanup each latch on their own line (tinytown-tnkuq.105's not-proven line)
description:
## What was seen

In fleet/controller/src/runs.rs (tinytown-tnkuq.105), a re-run the seam refuses — no project registered with the machine holds the run's record, the run directory's hash disagrees with the pin, the pack is not an installed layer, the bundle is gone — writes nothing to the stream. The pass folds the same run.waiting or run.could_not_tell on its next poll, asks again, and the refusal repeats on stderr every poll for as long as the record stands. The park (item.parked) and the cleanup (run.cleaned) both latch on a line of their own; a seam refusal does not. The builder named it in the delivery's not-proven line and the reviewer accepted it as a known limit.

## What this bead asks

Decide the shape and build it: either a refusal writes a lifecycle line the fold reads as terminal-until-something-changes (a run.refused or a could-not-tell row with the refusal as its read, counted toward the crash cap so the run parks like any other unreadable one), or the refusal parks the run outright with the refusal as the gate's reason. The recommendation is the first: a refused re-run is a fact about one execution attempt, and the cap already turns repeated ones into a park a person reads.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1 an arm in fleet/controller/tests/runs.rs whose stub refuses every re-run reads the same number of seam calls after ten passes as after the cap-plus-one, and one item.parked, and no further ask.
- AC2 the controller PRD's R35-R37 gain the sentence that says what a refused re-run does.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a scratch machine directory, write a stream whose last lifecycle line for a run is run.waiting, then append one unrelated line so the head passes the recorded position.
2. Drive fleet_controller::runs::tick with a Runs seam whose rerun answers Err (the test stub in fleet/controller/tests/runs.rs with an empty script does this).
3. Tick three more times: each pass asks the seam again and returns the same refusal; count the seam calls and read the stream — no line was written that the fold would read as a stop, which is the finding (compare the park, whose second pass asks nothing).

title: the provider-neutral policy layer's owning bead: move the five one-vendor keys out of controller policy and behind the adapter, including the posture word that is durable data
description:
## Why

Filed on Alberto's ruling D4:A off flight tinytown-tjgr7, 2026-09-17, which adopted "file the owning bead now, unscheduled" over dropping the requirement or leaving it for whoever starts the second adapter.

tinytown-tnkuq.27 measured that the controller's defaults name one AI vendor's models and posture values OUTSIDE the adapter, and that the plan document's own Q4 rules those belong to the adapter. It recorded the gap and priced the move; it did not own the fix, and the slice that was supposed to own it DOES NOT EXIST -- slices one through five are closed, no second-provider bead is on the board, and the PRD now describes this as the second adapter's prerequisite.

A prerequisite with no bead is one nothing will schedule. This bead is that bead, so the requirement stops being discoverable only by tripping over it.

## What is known, from tinytown-tnkuq.27's measurement rather than from this bead

Its 88-line section "What is the adapter's and what is the fleet's — corrected 2026-09-17" is the input, and these are its readings, each of which should be RE-MEASURED before being built on, because they were taken on 2026-09-17 and this repository lands commits continuously:

- Five one-vendor keys sit in the neutral policy layer, with a per-key table on that bead.
- A fleet.toml with no controller table is a fleet that has silently chosen one vendor.
- The adapter is constructed at FIVE production sites across two crates, not at the loop alone -- a correction tinytown-tnkuq.27 made against its own spec.
- THE POSTURE WORD IS DURABLE DATA, rebuilt from stored event payloads. So moving it changes the meaning of a field this work cannot rewrite in place, which is the part that makes this more than a refactor.
- One vendor has two spellings in the tree, claude_code and claude, with no cross-check between them.

## Acceptance criteria

Not written. This bead is filed UNSCHEDULED and unspecced by his ruling: its purpose today is that the prerequisite exists on the board and is findable. A spec pass writes acceptance when it is scheduled, and the spec pass owns deciding whether this is one bead or a spine -- the durable-data finding above is the reason it might be more than one.

## What this bead is NOT

It is not the second provider adapter, and it does not choose a second provider. It is the neutrality work the second adapter needs to have already happened.

title: WAIT_MS's floor is unproven in both directions and no signal-trap red-proof can reach it, because the kill it guards is an untrappable SIGKILL -- proving it needs a wrong-group miss instead
description:
WAIT_MS at fleet/cli/tests/drive_causes.rs:479 is the one constant among the four measured on tinytown-ul822 that buys correctness rather than calm: it is derived as STUB_SLEEP_MS + DRAIN_GRACE + START_COST_MARGIN_MS = 2700 ms, and a wait shorter than the stub's whole life passes on a kill that MISSED. Its floor is therefore the interesting number, and tinytown-ul822 could not measure it.

WHY THE RED-PROOF WAS UNAVAILABLE, and why that is structural rather than a builder's miss. The natural mutant is to make the kill miss and watch the arm stay green at a lower wait. tinytown-ul822's builder injected trap '' TERM into the kill arm's stub body, occurrence count 1 before and 1 after, and got 10 PASS at WAIT_MS 2700 and 10 PASS at 1200. It correctly declined to count that as a red: the mutant compiled and changed the subject but was NOT OBSERVABLE.

THE OPERATOR VERIFIED THE CAUSE AT SOURCE on base ceeba387abee02ae20c7ba5a4708dcb5da479e8d. fleet/controller/src/platform/mod.rs reads killpg(leader as i32, SIGKILL) inside kill_process_group, guarded only by an is_killable_group early return. SIGKILL cannot be trapped, so no signal disposition in the stub can make this kill miss. One correction to the delivery's wording: that call is not unconditional as it stated, since the is_killable_group guard sits above it -- the conclusion is unaffected, because untrappability is what does the work.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY PROVE THE FLOOR. A miss has to come from the kill reaching the WRONG process group rather than from a signal being ignored -- for instance a stub that escapes its group before the kill, or an is_killable_group false negative. tinytown-ul822 did not attempt this and said so in its not-proven line.

SO WHAT IS OPEN. The floor of WAIT_MS is unproven in both directions: nobody has shown 2700 ms is enough, and nobody has shown it is more than enough. It should not be lowered on a green, because at this site a green is the assertion looking away -- the same structural fact that made three of that bead's four ladders unable to red.

title: fleet/cli drive.rs: an_outrun_listing_is_reaped_and_not_left_a_zombie races /bin/sh start-up against its own 200 ms seam — the stub's pid file is read empty, measured 1 in 70 at base and 2 in 35 at the reviewed SHA
description:
## Why

Found by the reviewer's own full-suite run at tinytown-tnkuq.24.3's reviewed SHA (aff4001e6), which came back rc 2 — "891 tests run: 890 passed, 1 failed" — on this one arm, while the builder's run of the same SHA had been 891/891. The arm is `fleet-cli::drive unreadable_causes::an_outrun_listing_is_reaped_and_not_left_a_zombie`.

The panic, at `fleet/cli/tests/drive.rs:3761`:
    the stub writes one pid and nothing else, "": cannot parse integer from empty string

## The mechanism, read off the arm rather than guessed

The arm installs a stub `#!/bin/sh\necho $$ > '<pid_file>'\nsleep 2\necho '[]'\n` and runs it under a **200 ms** deadline (`Duration::from_millis(200)`), asserts the call was killed for not answering, then reads the pid the stub recorded. The shell's `>` redirect CREATES the file before `echo` writes to it, so an empty file means `/bin/sh` was started, reached the redirect, and was killed before the write landed. It is a race between `/bin/sh` process start-up and a 200 ms seam — the same family as tinytown-fq8p8 (the controller's drive.rs, a stub that never reaches its first line before the seam) and the load-sensitive drive arms tinytown-xlhq9, tinytown-yhpnn and tinytown-h1d16. tinytown-eg6gp covered a DIFFERENT defect in this same arm (a zombie count read too widely) and is closed; this is not that.

## The measurement, and it is why nothing was returned

Isolated runs, one arm at a time, on the same box, the base runs and the reviewed runs both taken after the box went quiet (the first reviewed sample was taken while load was still shedding and is reported separately below):

| tree | isolated runs | failures | rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| base 9e018d814 (tinytown-tnkuq.24.3 NOT applied) | 70 | 1 | ~1.4% |
| reviewed aff4001e6 | 35 | 2 | ~5.7% |

**The arm fails at the BASE**, without the guard slice, which is the reading that settles it: this is not a regression tinytown-tnkuq.24.3 introduced. Fisher's exact on 1/70 against 2/35 is about p=0.26 — the two rates are not distinguishable at this sample size, and I am not claiming they are equal, only that nothing here separates them. The reviewed sample includes one failure from a 5-run batch taken while the box still carried load from two concurrent suites, and one from a 30-run batch on a quiet box.

Mechanism agrees with the rates: tinytown-tnkuq.24.3's diff touches `fleet/cli/src/main.rs` only inside the `guard` command path (`Class::parse`'s message, `resolve_policy`, `caller_readings`, `guard::configured`, `with_targets`), and `drive` calls none of it. The whole diff's only occurrence of the string "drive" is the word "driven" in a doc comment.

## What lands

The 200 ms seam is the arm's subject and must stay, so the fix is not a longer deadline. Two shapes, measured against each other before one is chosen, on a run of at least 100 isolated iterations per side with the rate quoted:

A. **Witness the stub's start before the seam is armed.** The rig waits, bounded, for the stub to reach its first line (a marker file it writes before the pid) and only then starts the deadline, so the 200 ms measures what the arm means to measure — the call outrunning the deadline — rather than `/bin/sh`'s start-up plus that. Same shape tinytown-fq8p8 option B proposes for the controller.
B. **Read the pid as a three-way answer.** Absent file, empty file and a parsed pid are distinguished, and an empty file re-runs the call up to a bounded budget rather than panicking — the arm's subject is whether a reaped child is left a zombie, and it has no reading at all when the stub never wrote.

A is the better shape if the measurement supports it, because it removes the race rather than tolerating it; B is the honest fallback if start-up cannot be witnessed cheaply.

## Boundary

Not this bead: tinytown-fq8p8's controller-side retry budget, which is the same family on a different suite and has its own two shapes; any change to the 200 ms seam itself; the other load-sensitive drive arms, which are separately filed.

## Acceptance Criteria

• AC1 the chosen shape is implemented, and the arm run **at least 100 isolated iterations** on a quiet box with **zero** failures, the count and the command quoted.
• AC2 a control proving the arm can still fail for its real subject: with the reap deliberately removed, the arm goes RED naming the zombie — so the fix did not turn the arm into one that cannot fail.
• AC3 the seam stays 200 ms, asserted in the arm, so a future reader cannot mistake a widened deadline for a fix.
• AC4 `make fleet-test` rc 0 with the arm count before and after quoted; `make fleet-fmt` rc 0.

title: fleet: one reader of the item store, with the binary and the deadline as seams
description:
Two readers now make the identical call `bd -C <root> list -a <seat> --json`: fleet_core::store::Bd::assigned_to, and fleet/cli/src/prime.rs's own items(). They differ in the two properties a session-start hook needs and the general reader does not have — Bd runs `bd` BY BARE NAME (lessons claude-code D1 says a service PATH finds nothing) and waits on it with NO BOUND (a hook that hangs blocks the session start). prime therefore kept its own reader at tinytown-tnkuq.17 (its D8), which the reviewer may overrule.

The end state this bead is for: give core's Bd an injectable binary and a deadline, so one reader serves both callers. That means a constructor seam beside Bd::at, the resolution shape the claude adapter already uses (FLEET_*_BIN when absolute, else the constructed child PATH), platform::run_bounded in place of the bare output() call — which puts a controller dependency in front of core, so the bound may have to be handed in rather than taken — and Row gaining the title prime's line carries. Every current caller of Store::assigned_to (fleet/cli/src/item.rs) moves with it.

Not urgent: both readers are correct today. This is convergence, and it is the third option D8 named and declined as wider than a rebase.

title: The review panel returns as a fleet feature after the migration — what the experiment measured and what the feature has to carry
description:
## Why

Alberto's ruling on the parent epic: the panel comes back after the fleet migration, as a feature of fleet that makes it work correctly. This bead holds what the experiment measured so the fleet design starts from it and not from memory; it is blocked on the fleet epic.

## What the experiment measured (2026-09-02 to 2026-09-07, from the record)

- 99 panel tables over 81 beads; 46 full panels, 11 four-lens, 8 single-lens; every full panel on an executable diff — the sizer never sent a comment-only delivery to a panel.
- The lens contract worked: every lane returned one validated object and proved its tree read-only; DEGRADED never fired for a budget because the ceiling never reached the call (budget.total null on every invocation).
- The refutation stage worked as a filter: on the fleet flights the high rows were refuted 0/2 more often than confirmed, and the two returns it produced (tinytown-r87hb, tinytown-uy8ls) were real defects a reviewer had not seen.
- What failed: the cost was a property of the trigger, not of the diff — the fleet label read its own economy level (LG) and rule R2 fired on any test-only delivery, so a 17-line constant pin drew a five-lane panel; each panel produced 10 to 38 rows, and under R2 the non-defect rows became one or two luggage beads carrying the fleet label, each drawing a panel of its own; the panel's cost line counted agent tokens (0.6 to 2.1M) where the bill was input re-reads (about 250M billed input per panelled fleet bead against 84M for the one architect-read bead on the same flight); each fan-out left seven lane worktrees under the primary (260 at retirement, tinytown-on3df).

## What the fleet feature should carry

- The trigger is the diff, never a label or a global level: executable lines in product code.
- Lanes run as fleet seats with their own accounting, so the bill is read from the seats' rows and not from a workflow's token field.
- Rows that are not defects are folded into one rolling coverage record per file, never one bead per landing.
- Lane worktrees are the fleet's to create and reap.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Written when the fleet migration closes; until then this bead is the record.
notes:
FOLDED IN at Alberto's board triage (2026-09-07, architect-2's session; his word: close the panel-stale beads and keep the findings where the fleet feature reads them). Two requirements the panel experiment measured, carried here so the returning feature starts from them:
(1) from tinytown-bqbyl (closed): a lens fan-out put the fleet's one shared box under synthetic load to test a timing claim — 24 concurrent yes processes and a six-way python hog from the refuter lane over tinytown-okj2a on 2026-09-07, load 163, during other seats' hours. The feature bounds what a lens may run on the shared box: no synthetic load above a stated ceiling, no fan-out wider than the box's measured width, and a timing claim is refuted by reading the arm's own bound and not by hogging the machine.
(2) from tinytown-mhqyk (closed): tools/review-size's delta row picked the delivery a re-delivery REPLACES by walking the bead's markers and taking the last resolvable sha other than the sized one, so a marker written after the sized delivery's own could be taken as the one it replaced. While the panel is disabled the delta row moves nothing; when the feature returns, the "previous delivery" is read from the return note's own sha, never from marker order.

title: fleet core test sweep: a store whose pid an unrelated live process reused reads alive under kill -0 and is never swept
description:
## Why

Filed off tinytown-neyaw on run tinytown-hjbpz under the operator's decision tinytown-hjbpz-D2. The scratch-store sweep judges a store's owner alive with kill -0 on the pid in its name, as the spec prescribed. A pid the OS has reused for an unrelated long-lived process reads alive, so that store survives: measured on this box, fleet-store-dispatch-73816-0 (created Sep 8) and fleet-store-dispatch-24260-0 (created Sep 9), whose pids ps -p named as StatusKitAgent and a dart tooling daemon. The sweep otherwise works (403 fleet-store-* to 4 on the first run).

## What

Unspecced. Make liveness mean "the process that created this store": e.g. compare the process's start time (ps -o lstart, or /proc/<pid>/stat on Linux) with the store directory's creation time, or put a start-time token in the store name. Platform-specific; must keep the never-remove-blind rule (a check that cannot run answers alive).

## Acceptance Criteria

To be written at the spec pass. Minimum: a store whose pid is reused by an unrelated live process is removed, and a live run's store is kept, each by a named arm.
notes:
Measured on flight tinytown-hjbpz (operator probe, tinytown-neyaw at 9045b8a77): the sweep's kill -0 treats EPERM as dead. A store named with pid 1 (root's launchd) was REMOVED by a non-root run, while a store named with a live same-user pid (the test's parent) was kept. On macOS that is correct (TMPDIR is per-user, so a pid held by another user cannot be the store's creator); on a shared Linux /tmp it would sweep another user's LIVE store. The spec pass for this bead should decide EPERM's meaning alongside start-time liveness.

title: fleet core add: after the atomic lock write, pin's read-back has no reaching arm and its doc comment names a case that can no longer occur
description:
## Why

Filed off tinytown-wzdbn on run tinytown-hjbpz, under the operator's decision tinytown-hjbpz-D1 (Option A): packs.lock is now written by temp-and-rename, which replaces a symlinked lock, so the one arm that reached add's read-back (a lock symlinked to /dev/null) was re-pointed to pin the replacement, and no arm reaches the read-back any more. The builder left fleet/core/src/add.rs untouched (its D9, accepted), so the doc comment on the pin write (add.rs:301-304 at 092bce6ab) still names "a lock path that swallows its bytes" as a case the read-back catches — a case that can no longer occur. "A filesystem that lied" still can, in principle.

## What

Unspecced; a small decision first: keep Refusal::LockDidNotLand (add.rs:95, :151, :309) as defence against a filesystem that reports a write it did not keep, correcting the comment to that case alone and naming it as reached by no arm; or delete the read-back as closed by construction. Either way the comment stops naming the symlink case.

## Acceptance Criteria

To be written at the spec pass; minimum: the pin doc comment names no case the atomic write rules out, verified by reading it against lock::write.
